issues.explanation: Occupation 'Retired' is implausible for age 28 (retired is implausible if age < 50).

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits awkwardly with 'my memories are very clear and detailed' and 'mostly pictures or images' for a PTSD profile tied to a life-threatening accident; this pattern suggests unusually easy verbal processing despite vivid intrusive-style memory, which weakens coherence of the memory node.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat item about repeatedly checking whether someone is following him implies an interpersonal pursuit/assault-type danger theme, which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being a life-threatening accident and with the rest of the profile, which does not otherwise indicate persecution-related threat.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'I dwell on what other people have done to me' also implies an interpersonal harm/blame theme that does not fit well with the accident trauma context or the other selected appraisals, memories, and threats.

issues.item: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other items describe accident-related sensory threat (loud sounds, startle), image-based trauma memory, and self-critical appraisals, with maladaptive responses centered on avoidance/removal from reminders and rumination/meaning seeking. Undereating introduces a qualitatively different coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in Triggers, Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, making it the least clinically coherent item in this five-component profile.

vignette:
David, a 52-year-old film director of European descent, had built his career on being able to orchestrate chaos into controlled, beautiful frames. That had changed one night, about fourteen months ago, when he was driving home from a late location scout through a winding coastal road. His headlights caught the eyes of a deer just as another vehicle crested the hill ahead. He swerved, the car left the asphalt, rolled twice, and came to rest upside down in a dry ditch. He remembered the shriek of tearing metal, the glass exploding inward, and then the dark-absolute, suffocating, smelling of gasoline and damp soil. He had been trapped in the overturned car for nearly forty minutes, suspended by his seatbelt, unable to see anything, hearing only the hiss of the engine and the distant sound of someone shouting his name. When the rescuers finally cut him out, he was covered in blood from a scalp wound, but physically intact. The paramedics said he was lucky. David did not feel lucky.

In the months that followed, David found that he could not shake the images. The memory of the accident was not a story he could tell; it came as a series of vivid snapshots-the glare of headlights, the dashboard crumpling toward his chest, the taste of copper and dust. If he tried to describe it to his partner, the words felt hollow, as though the real event existed only in pictures his mind could not translate into language. He found himself jumping at ordinary sounds: the clatter of a dropped coffee cup on set, the hiss of a pressure valve, even the sharp crack of a director's slate. Each time, his heart would lurch, and he would feel a flush of shame. He had come to believe that his reactions proved something damning about him-that he was a lousy coper, that he was fundamentally inadequate, that the person he had become was unrecognisable to himself. A man who once relished the controlled chaos of production now startled at his own assistant's voice.

David's work as a director forced him into environments thick with sudden noises and unpredictable lighting, and he had begun to adapt in ways that worried his crew. He insisted on keying every scene with at least a three-quarter fill light; no shadows, no darkness, even when the script called for a moonlit bedroom. He had a standing rule that no one could approach him from behind without verbal warning. He stopped attending night shoots altogether, claiming creative differences, but really because the darkness outside the soundstage triggered a visceral sense of being trapped in that overturned car. Instead, he buried himself in post-production-spending twelve-hour days in the editing bay, headphones on, cutting and colour-grading, anything to keep his mind occupied. The distraction worked, but it came at a cost. His partner had begun to feel shut out; dinners were cancelled, weekends disappeared into the cutting room. David knew he was hiding, but the alternative-sitting alone with his thoughts, drifting into the why of it all-felt worse. He would catch himself asking why this had happened to him, as if the universe had singled him out, and then he would push the question away with another task.

What finally brought David to seek help was a meeting with his producer, who told him bluntly that his avoidance of night shoots was costing the studio money and that his behaviour on set had become "a liability." David had snapped at a sound engineer who dropped a sandbag, and the incident had spread through the small film community. His partner had also sat him down and said she didn't recognise him anymore-those were his own words, echoing back. He was terrified that he was ruining the career he had spent thirty years building, and even more terrified that if he stopped and really looked at the accident, he would find something even worse: proof that he was, after all, a man who could not handle what life threw at him. He sat in the therapist's office with his hands clasped, and for a long moment he said nothing. Then he looked up and said, quietly, "I used to know exactly what scene we were shooting. Now I just want to know who I'm supposed to be."
